narrative:
The model predicts you have a 59% chance of failing your final year, which is why the school requires you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this outlook were your plans for higher education, your history with past classes, and the amount of time you spend studying each week. Wanting to pursue higher education is actually the strongest influence working in your favor; almost every student who passed expressed the same ambition, and the model sees this as a clear sign of motivation that pulls your chances toward passing. However, two other elements pushed harder in the opposite direction. Your limited weekly study time—under two hours—stands out because most students who passed dedicated noticeably more time, typically between two and five hours. This lack of regular study proved to be a significant drag on the prediction. In addition, although you have not failed any classes before, the absence of any prior setbacks did not provide the model with the reassuring signal it often sees in successful students.

To turn this around, focus first on building a consistent study routine of at least two hours most days. Protect that time as seriously as you protect your desire to continue studying after school. Small, steady increases in effort there can shift your outlook quickly and may even remove the need for remedial classes next term.
